title: Agile sustainability and scaling agile
blurb: Recall agile sustainability as a transformation success factor and explain what scaling agile means and how PRINCE2 Agile keeps many teams aligned and governed.
question: What does scaling up agile enable an organization to do, according to PRINCE2 Agile?

teach.body: Agile sustainability is the third success factor of agile transformations in the syllabus, with agile maturity and psychological safety, and one of the key metrics for agility measured in agile maturity assessments. Put simply, it asks whether agile ways of working will last: are they embedded in the culture, kept up at a pace people can maintain, and safe from being rolled back once the transformation team moves on?

teach.h: The three success factors and key metrics

teach.body: Several parts of PRINCE2 Agile point the same way. Being agile, not just doing agile, brings a cultural shift and long-term resilience. When detailing the change management approach, the book says to consider the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation. The agile coach helps organizations adopt and sustain agile principles and practices. And the Agile Manifesto asks for sustainable development: sponsors, developers and users able to keep a constant pace indefinitely.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.3.1, 4.2.1, Table 7.2; Agile Manifesto principles

teach.body: Scaling up agile means adopting agile values and principles beyond small teams, to support larger, multi-team and multi-product environments. It lets an organization keep agility across many teams, aligning them to shared goals and streamlined processes, so complex initiatives gain agile flexibility, collaboration and responsiveness while keeping sufficient governance and control. It is not about short-term goals, a single team, or re-creating governance separately for each team.

teach.h: Who does what when agile scales
head: Role
Scope in a scaled project
rows: One for the project; agrees work with each PO
Across teams; owns the project backlog, sets priorities
One team; owns its product backlog, aligned to project backlog
Works with one or two teams
Across the organization; removes systemic blockers

teach.body: With several teams there may be several product owners, but still one project manager. The chief product owner represents the user community, owns the project backlog and keeps it aligned with the teams' product backlogs, setting priorities across teams, such as consistent branding for every team's output. Each product owner owns one team's product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog. Team composition is the same as in a single-team project.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1, Figure 7.2, Table 7.2

steps.label: Product backlogs
steps.sub: one per team; owned by POs

teach.body: Orrin Home Stores is moving its website, app and in-store tills onto one loyalty scheme, with three delivery teams. Project manager Leon Brandt agrees work packages with each team's product owner. Chief product owner Fatima Shah prioritizes across the teams so the loyalty branding and rules match everywhere. To make the change last, the change management approach covers how the culture will evolve, and the teams keep a pace they can sustain rather than sprinting to each release.

teach.text: Agile sustainability is not the sustainability performance target. The target is about the project's impact on the wider environment (fixed at minimum criteria, flexed above). Agile sustainability is a transformation success factor about agility lasting. And scaling keeps governance; it does not rebuild it for every team.

items: Agile sustainability: a success factor and key metric, about agile ways of working lasting.
Make change stick: evolve the culture and ensure changes are not rolled back; keep a sustainable pace.
Scaling up agile: agile values and principles beyond small teams, for multi-team and multi-product work.
Scaling aligns teams to shared goals and streamlined processes while keeping sufficient governance and control.
At scale: one project manager, a CPO across teams owning the project backlog, a PO per team, team coaches for one or two teams.

summary: You can now recall agile sustainability as a success factor of agile transformations, distinct from the sustainability performance target, and say what helps agile changes last. You can also explain scaling up agile and how one project manager, a chief product owner and per-team product owners keep many teams aligned and governed.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The syllabus names agile maturity, psychological safety and agile [?] as success factors of agile transformations.
options: scaling
accountability
sustainability
velocity
A.why: The three success factors are agile maturity, psychological safety and agile sustainability (2.7.3 to 2.7.5).

whyNot.0: Scaling is a separate topic about multi-team and multi-product agility.
whyNot.1: Accountability matters in governance, but it is not one of the three named success factors.
whyNot.3: Velocity is a delivery measure, not a transformation success factor.

A.q: Which statement describes scaling up agile in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Speeding up a single team by adding more members to it
Taking agile values beyond small teams to many teams
Giving each team its own separate governance arrangements
Focusing teams on short-term delivery goals
A.why: Scaling up agile means adopting agile values and principles beyond small teams to support multi-team and multi-product environments (3.2).

whyNot.0: Scaling focuses on multi-team environments, not a single team.
whyNot.2: Governance is maintained across teams, not re-created for each one.
whyNot.3: Short-term goals are not the focus of scaling up agile.

A.q: In a PRINCE2 Agile project with several delivery teams, which role sets priorities across the teams?
options: Team product owner
Project executive
Project manager
Chief product owner
A.why: The chief product owner owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams (Table 7.2, Figure 7.2).

whyNot.0: A product owner owns one team's product backlog and does not prioritize across teams.
whyNot.1: The project executive is accountable for the project but does not own the backlogs or set cross-team priorities.
whyNot.2: The project manager runs the project day to day; the CPO sets cross-team priorities.

B.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, what does scaling up agile enable an organization to do?
options: Align many teams to shared goals while keeping governance
Let each team set its own goals without central control
Replace the project board with team-level decisions
Focus every team on its own short-term targets
B.why: Scaling keeps agility across teams, aligning them to shared goals and streamlined processes while maintaining sufficient governance and control (3.2).

whyNot.1: Scaling aligns teams to shared goals; it does not drop governance.
whyNot.2: Governance and control are kept; the project board is not replaced.
whyNot.3: Scaling is not about short-term goals but about alignment across teams.

B.q: A board member says 'agile sustainability' means the project's impact on the wider environment. Which response is correct?
options: Correct: it is one of the seven performance targets
Correct: it is fixed at minimum criteria in fix and flex
Incorrect: that is the sustainability performance target
Incorrect: it describes the delivery team's velocity trend
B.why: Impact on the wider environment is the sustainability performance target (1.3.2). Agile sustainability is a success factor of agile transformations and a key metric for agility (2.7.5, 2.7.6).

whyNot.0: Sustainability is one of the seven performance targets, but that target is different from agile sustainability.
whyNot.1: Fixed at minimum criteria describes the sustainability performance target in fix and flex.
whyNot.3: Velocity is a delivery measure, not agile sustainability.

B.q: Which structure is typical for a PRINCE2 Agile project with several delivery teams?
options: A project manager per team and one chief product owner
One project manager, a CPO, and a product owner per team
One project manager and a chief product owner per team
One product owner for all teams and no team coaches
B.why: Multi-team projects have one project manager, possibly several product owners, and one CPO prioritizing across teams (7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

whyNot.0: There is one project manager for the project, not one per team.
whyNot.2: The CPO works across teams; each team has a product owner.
whyNot.3: Each team keeps its usual composition, including a product owner and coaching.

C.q:
Which two statements about scaling agile in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Scaling keeps sufficient governance and control.
2. Scaling means each team re-creates its own governance.
3. The CPO keeps the project backlog aligned with the teams' product backlogs.
4. Each product owner sets priorities across all the teams.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Scaling maintains sufficient governance and control (1), and the CPO keeps the project backlog aligned with team product backlogs (3) (3.2, Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: governance is maintained, not re-created for each team.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: governance is not rebuilt per team, and cross-team priorities belong to the CPO.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a product owner owns one team's backlog; the CPO prioritizes across teams.

C.q: An organization wants its new agile ways of working to stick after the transformation team leaves. According to PRINCE2 Agile, what should the change management approach consider?
options: The evolving culture and how to stop changes being rolled back
Bonus payments for staff who adopt the agile ways of working
A single launch announcement to all staff about the change
A stricter audit of each team's compliance with agile rules
C.why: The book says to consider the evolving culture and ways to ensure changes are not rolled back after the transformation (4.2.1).

whyNot.1: Financial incentives cannot by themselves guarantee that changes stay in place.
whyNot.2: One announcement informs people but does not embed the change in the culture.
whyNot.3: Compliance audits enforce rules but do not evolve the culture that keeps agility going.

C.q: At Calloway Bank, four delivery teams are building parts of a new savings app. The bank wants the same branding across every team's screens. Who should set this as a priority, and why?
options: The chief product owner, as they prioritize across teams
Each product owner, as each owns a product backlog
The agile coach, as they work across the organization
The project executive, as they are accountable for the project
C.why: The CPO represents the users, owns the project backlog and sets priorities across teams, such as consistent branding (Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: Each PO owns one team's backlog; separate POs would not ensure consistency across teams.
whyNot.2: The agile coach removes systemic blockers to agile adoption; they do not set product priorities.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable for the project, but cross-team product priorities belong to the CPO.

reteach.title: An orchestra, not a solo
reteach.question: How does PRINCE2 Agile keep agility going and growing?

blocks.body: Scaling agile is like growing from a soloist to an orchestra: each section (team) has its own lead (product owner), one conductor sets the shared score (the chief product owner across teams), and the concert still runs to the venue's rules (governance). Agile sustainability is whether the orchestra is still playing well next season, at a pace the musicians can keep, rather than reverting to old habits.

blocks.text: Two traps in one topic: agile sustainability is not the environmental sustainability target, and scaling does not create separate governance for each team.

explain.body: Agile sustainability is a success factor of agile transformations and a key metric for agility, assessed through agile maturity assessments (2.7.5, 2.7.6, 12.4.1).

test.q: Through which technique is agile sustainability assessed as a key metric for agility?
options: Cumulative flow diagrams
Agile maturity assessments
Burn-down charts
Team skill matrices
test.why: Agile maturity assessments are based on the key metrics for agility: psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (12.4.1).

whyNot.0: Cumulative flow diagrams show work states and bottlenecks.
whyNot.2: Burn-down charts show work remaining over time.
whyNot.3: Team skill matrices show capabilities and training needs.

explain.body: The Agile Manifesto principles ask for sustainable development: sponsors, developers and users able to keep a constant pace indefinitely.

test.q: Which Agile Manifesto principle says sponsors, developers and users should be able to keep up a constant pace indefinitely?
options: Welcoming changing requirements
Simplicity in the work done
Sustainable development
Self-organizing teams
test.why: The Manifesto principle on sustainable development says sponsors, developers and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.

whyNot.0: This principle is about welcoming change, even late in development.
whyNot.1: Simplicity is about maximizing the work not done.
whyNot.3: This principle is about the best designs emerging from self-organizing teams.

explain.body: Agile values and principles beyond small teams, for multi-team and multi-product work, aligned to shared goals with sufficient governance (3.2).

test.q: What does PRINCE2 Agile say is maintained when agile is scaled up?
options: Sufficient governance and control
One product owner for all teams
Separate goals for each team
A single team's working rhythm
test.why: Scaling up agile keeps agility across teams while maintaining sufficient governance and control (3.2).

whyNot.1: Several product owners are possible, one per team.
whyNot.2: Scaling aligns teams to shared goals, not separate ones.
whyNot.3: Scaling concerns multi-team environments, not one team.

explain.body: One project manager; a CPO across teams owning the project backlog; a product owner per team owning its product backlog; team coaches for one or two teams (7.3.1, Figure 7.2).

explain.caption: Priorities flow from the project backlog to team backlogs.

test.q: Which backlog does a product owner own in a scaled PRINCE2 Agile project?
options: The project backlog for all teams
The project backlog, jointly with the CPO
The backlog of every team in turn
The product backlog for one team
test.why: Each product owner owns their team's product backlog and keeps it aligned with the project backlog (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The project backlog is owned by the chief product owner.
whyNot.1: The CPO owns the project backlog; each PO owns its own team's product backlog and keeps it aligned.
whyNot.2: A PO owns one team's backlog, not every team's in rotation.
